bib.title: High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation

question: How can policy gradient estimates be made lower-variance and more sample-efficient, with tolerable bias, so neural-network policies learn high-dimensional continuous control?
hypothesis: An exponentially weighted average of k-step advantage estimates (GAE) with intermediate lambda gives a better bias-variance tradeoff than either one-step TD residuals or full Monte Carlo returns.
contributions: Justification and intuition for generalized advantage estimation (GAE), a variance reduction scheme for policy gradients; the formula was proposed earlier but the analysis is new and applies to batch trust-region algorithms.
A trust region method for optimizing the value function, found robust and efficient for neural network value functions.
Combining the two gives an algorithm that learns neural network policies for challenging control tasks, extending the state of the art in high-dimensional continuous control.

method.summary: GAE(gamma, lambda) computes advantages as the (gamma*lambda)-discounted sum of TD residuals from a learned value function. Policy is updated with TRPO and the value function is fit by Monte Carlo regression under a trust region (conjugate gradient). Evaluated on cart-pole and MuJoCo 3D biped, quadruped and stand-up tasks, varying gamma and lambda.

datasets.name: Cart-pole balancing
datasets.source: physical parameters from Barto et al. (1983)

datasets.name: 3D biped locomotion (MuJoCo)
datasets.preprocessing: episode terminated at 2000 timesteps or if centre of mass below 0.8 m; timestep 0.01 s

datasets.name: 3D quadruped locomotion (MuJoCo)
datasets.preprocessing: terminated if centre of mass below 0.2 m; 2000 timestep cap

datasets.name: Biped getting up (MuJoCo)
datasets.source: MuJoCo; biped starts lying on its back

models.name: Policy network (3D tasks)
models.params: inferred: over 10^4 (paper says each of policy and value net has over 10^4 parameters)
models.architecture: feedforward, tanh hidden units, linear output layer

models.name: Value network (3D tasks)
models.architecture: same as policy but one scalar output

models.name: Cart-pole policy and value
models.architecture: linear policy; value net with one 20-unit hidden layer

training.objective: Policy: TRPO, minimize L(theta) = (1/N) sum pi_theta/pi_old * A_hat subject to mean KL(pi_old, pi_theta) <= epsilon. Value: minimize sum ||V_phi(s_n) - V_hat_n||^2 subject to (1/N) sum ||V_phi - V_phi_old||^2 / (2 sigma^2) <= epsilon, V_hat = discounted return.
training.optimizer: TRPO natural-gradient step; value function trust region solved approximately with conjugate gradient
training.batch_size: cart-pole 20 trajectories; biped 50000 timesteps; quadruped and stand-up 200000 timesteps
training.steps: biped 1000 iterations (learning curves 500 shown); quadruped 1000 iterations in plot; cart-pole 50 iterations in plot
training.regularisation: trust region on value function to avoid overfitting latest batch
training.hardware: biped: 16-core machine; quadruped and stand-up: 32-core machine
training.wall_clock: about 2 hours per trial (biped, 16 cores); about 4 hours per trial (quadruped / stand-up, 32 cores)
training.seeds: cart-pole 21; biped 9; quadruped and stand-up 5 per condition

other.update_order: policy update uses V_phi_i (before value update) for advantages; updating value first adds bias

inference.samples: simulate current policy until N timesteps per iteration

baselines: No VF: time-dependent baseline averaging return at each timestep over the batch
eval.protocol: learning curves averaged over random seeds; gamma and lambda swept on cart-pole and biped, limited sweep on quadruped and stand-up; no significance test

evidence.where: Section 6.2.2 reward table (biped); quadruped: vfwd - 1e-6||u||^2 - 1e-3||f_impact||^2 + 0.05; stand-up: -(h_head - 1.5)^2 - 1e-5||u||^2

results.claim: GAE is the (gamma*lambda)-discounted sum of TD residuals delta_t = r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t); lambda=0 gives the one-step TD residual, lambda=1 gives empirical return minus V(s_t).
results.setup: Definition, Eq. 16-18, undiscounted problem with gamma as a variance-reduction parameter

results.claim: Best cart-pole results come at intermediate gamma and lambda.
results.setup: Cart-pole, linear policy, 20-unit value net, TRPO, 21 seeds
results.quote: indicate that the best results are obtained at intermediate values of the parameters: γ ∈[0.96, 0.99] and λ ∈[0.92, 0.99].
results.note: Fig 2 caption gives the fastest-improvement lambda range as [0.92, 0.98] at gamma = 0.99.

results.claim: Best 3D biped results come at intermediate gamma and lambda.
results.setup: 3D biped, 3-layer 100/50/25 tanh nets, TRPO, 50000 timesteps per batch, 9 seeds
results.quote: The best performance is again obtained using intermediate values of γ ∈[0.99, 0.995], λ ∈
results.note: The lambda range [0.96, 0.99] is split onto the next line in the text.

results.claim: Simulated experience for the 3D biped to learn to walk equals about 5.8 days of real time.
results.note: The abstract says the amount of simulated experience for 3D bipeds corresponds to 1-2 weeks of real time; text computes 5.8 days for biped locomotion.

results.claim: Recommended lambda range in the discussion.
results.quote: choosing an appropriate intermediate value of λ in the range [0.9, 0.99] usually results in the best performance.

results.claim: Best lambda is much lower than best gamma, because lambda adds bias only when V is inaccurate, while gamma < 1 always biases the gradient.
results.setup: Explanation of empirical finding; not tested separately
results.quote: Empirically, we ﬁnd that the best value of λ is much lower than the best value of γ, likely because λ introduces far less bias than γ for a reasonably accurate value function.

results.claim: The one-step return (lambda = 0) gave excessive bias and poor performance.
results.quote: While we found empirically that the one-step return (λ = 0) leads to excessive bias and poor performance

results.claim: On quadruped, lambda = 0.96 with a value function was best; on stand-up the value function always helped and lambda 0.96 and 1 were roughly equal.
results.setup: gamma fixed at 0.995 (quadruped legend) / 0.99 (stand-up legend); lambda in {0, 0.96} stated, plots also show lambda=1 and no value fn
results.quote: For 3D standing, the value function always helped, but the results are roughly the same for λ = 0.96 and λ = 1.
results.note: Text says lambda varied over {0, 0.96}; Fig 3/4 legends show 0.96, 1 and no value fn.

results.claim: Reward shaping with Phi = V gives the GAE: the (gamma*lambda)-discounted sum of shaped rewards equals the GAE; shaping leaves A^{pi,gamma} unchanged.

limits: Authors call the analysis of advantage estimation 'intuitive but informal'.
Quadruped and stand-up got only a limited gamma/lambda comparison because of compute cost.
Relationship between value function error and policy gradient error is left open; adaptive choice of gamma and lambda is future work.
Shared policy/value architecture left open; no convergence guarantees.
No comparison against deterministic-policy-gradient approaches (Lillicrap 2015; Heess 2015), which use lower-dimensional problems.
TRPO and value-function trust-region epsilon values, and learning rates, are not reported; no code release stated.
Seeds vary by task (21, 9, 5); no confidence intervals or significance tests described.

terms.definition: An advantage estimator that does not introduce bias when used in place of A^{pi,gamma} in the discounted policy gradient (Definition 1).
Exponentially-weighted average of k-step advantage estimators, equal to sum_l (gamma*lambda)^l delta^V_{t+l}.
chi(l; s_t, a_t) = E[r_{t+l} | s_t, a_t] - E[r_{t+l} | s_t]; A^{pi,gamma}(s,a) = sum_l gamma^l chi(l; s, a).
